blocks.text: In an RLC parallel circuit the resistor, inductor and capacitor are connected in parallel to each other across an AC source (Fig 17.12 a). The parallel arrangement changes the overall impedance and the way the current is shared, making it different from the series circuit.

items: Resonance and impedance: a parallel RLC circuit resonates when XL = XC, and then its impedance is at its maximum and it behaves like a purely resistive circuit. The impedance is Z = 1 / square root of [(1/R)^2 + (1/XL - 1/XC)^2] (17.27).

Voltage and current: the voltage is the same across every component, so it is taken as the reference phasor. At resonance the line current from the source is a minimum (Fig 17.12 b), while the branch currents IL and IC can each be larger than it; this can be used for current magnification.
Admittance: the admittance Y is the reciprocal of impedance, Y = 1/Z; the total admittance of a parallel circuit is the sum of the admittances of its branches.

Frequency and bandwidth: the impedance, admittance and currents all depend on frequency; the bandwidth is the range of frequencies over which the circuit works effectively. The resonant frequency is fr = 1/(2 pi square root of (LC)).
Quality factor (Q): a measure of the sharpness of the resonance peak, comparing the energy stored in the circuit with the energy dissipated.
Power factor: it varies with frequency and the relative sizes of the reactances; at resonance it is 1.

blocks.title: Q of a parallel circuit
blocks.text: The book says that in a parallel RLC circuit the Q-factor is inversely proportional to the resistance. For a parallel circuit the opposite is true: Q = R square root of (C/L), which increases with R (a larger parallel resistance wastes less current). It is in a series circuit, Q = (1/R) square root of (L/C), that Q falls as R rises. Flagged for review.

blocks.alt: Left: an AC source with a resistor R, an inductor L and a capacitor C each connected directly across it as separate branches; the same voltage is across every branch. Right: a graph of line current against frequency that falls to a minimum at the resonant frequency fr and rises again on both sides; at resonance the impedance is largest and the line current smallest.
blocks.caption: RLC parallel circuit and its current dip at resonance (original diagram after Fig 17.12).
blocks.long_description: At resonance the inductor and capacitor currents are equal and opposite, so they cancel in the supply wires: energy swings between them while the source supplies only the small current needed by R.

blocks.text: Parallel RLC circuits are used in tuning circuits, signal processing and power systems. In induction cooktops (Fig 17.12 c, a photograph), the resonance of a parallel RLC circuit drives a high-frequency current in the coil, which induces currents in the metal cookware and heats it.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is used to diagnose heart conditions by recording the small electric waves generated during heart activity, displayed on a cathode-ray oscilloscope or screen.

blocks.prompt: How does the line current at resonance differ between series and parallel RLC circuits?
blocks.explanation: In a series circuit the impedance is a minimum (Z = R), so the current is a maximum; in a parallel circuit the impedance is a maximum, so the line current is a minimum.

items: Parallel RLC: same voltage on each branch; Z = 1/sqrt((1/R)^2 + (1/XL - 1/XC)^2).
Resonance (XL = XC): Z maximum, line current minimum; fr = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)).
Admittance Y = 1/Z; uses: tuning, induction cooktops.
